B.6 SEWAGE SLUDGE | HTL | RD This study assumes a centralized HTL biocrude upgrading plant, with the capacity of processing 110 dry tons of waste feedstocks per day and producing 2,700 barrels per stream day (BPSD) of biofuel blendstocks. The HTL biocrude upgrading process mainly includes hydrotreating and hydrocracking to remove the heteroatoms in the biocrude. Specifically, the biocrude feed is first pumped to 10.5 MPa, mixed with compressed hydrogen, and preheated to the hydrotreater reactor temperature of 400°C. The hydrotreating process can convert biocrude oxygen, nitrogen, and sulfur into CO and water, ammonia, and hydrogen sulfide, respectively. The hydrotreater effluent 2 is cooled to 25°C to separate the gas and water. The resulting hydrocarbons are then fractionated into lights, naphtha, diesel, and heavy oil. Heavy oil combined with hydrogen is then hydrocracked at 400°C and 7 MPa to increase diesel yield. Hydrogen is produced onsite via steam reforming of the upgrading off-gas and purchased natural gas. B.7 SWINE MANURE | HTL | RD The conversion process and plant scale are the same as RD: sludge HTL, but high-moisture-content swine manure is used. Swine farms produce solid waste at a much slower rate than the typical wastewater treatment plant. It is reported that 90% of swine farms in the United States can generate <2 dry ton of recoverable swine manure per day, per farm. Thus, swine manure collection and transportation cost would be more expensive than the wastewater sludge. HTL refineries, co- located with a large wastewater treatment plant, can potentially receive credits due to the avoided disposal cost at $40/wet ton sludge. The swine manure cost at the gate of the HTL plant is assumed to be zero in the analysis, assuming potential avoided disposal cost to farms and transportation cost offset the swine manure collection and transportation cost to support the 110 tons per day HTL plant scale. B-2 B.8 WOODY BIOMASS | CFP (PT/TIO ) | RD 2 The bio-oil produced from biomass CFP technology is sent to an existing petroleum refinery with hydrotreating and hydrocracking capabilities to be upgraded into renewable hydrocarbon fuel blendstocks, including renewable diesel. B.9 WOODY BIOMASS | GASIFICATION | METHANOL Similar to the FT pathway, biomass is first converted to syngas in a gasifier, followed by tar reforming, amine-based syngas cleanup and steam reforming (Tan et al., 2015; Zhu et al., 2009). The clean syngas, with a desired H /CO ratio of 2, is then compressed and sent to the methanol 2 synthesis reactor filled with Zn-Cu catalyst to produce crude methanol, which is purified by distillation to generate high purity methanol. Due to the relatively low per-pass conversion of the methanol synthesis reaction, unconverted syngas is recycled back to the reactor to boost overall conversion.
